chapter_title: Implementing OCP: Design Patterns and Abstractions

screens.title: Implementing OCP: Design Patterns and Abstractions
screens.subtitle: Make your code closed to modification but open to extension using polymorphism, patterns, and DI.

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on the practical techniques that turn the Open/Closed Principle from an idea into working code. You will learn why depending on abstractions matters, how polymorphism creates extension points, and how patterns like Strategy and Template Method implement OCP in real systems. We will also cover Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control as the mechanisms that let you swap implementations without changing clients. Through short Java code walkthroughs and a hands-on shipping cost activity, you will see concrete refactor steps: introduce an interface, create concrete implementations, and inject them into a context. We emphasize where not to over-abstract and how to choose the right places to apply OCP. By the end you'll be able to identify candidates for OCP, refactor a conditional-mess into a strategy-based design, and understand how DI supports testing and extension. As you move through the lesson, look for the recurring pattern: define an abstraction, implement variations, and let the client depend only on the abstraction. How might you identify the first class in your codebase that needs this change?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Depend on abstractions, not implementations: create extension points with interfaces or abstract classes, and use DI to provide concrete strategies at runtime.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will: first, use polymorphism and abstraction to create extension points that keep classes closed for modification. You will practice converting concrete conditionals into interface-based designs and understand the practical trade-offs. Second, apply the Strategy Pattern to make algorithms interchangeable at runtime. You will see how to define a strategy interface, implement concrete strategies, and have a context delegate behavior. Third, understand the Template Method Pattern and how a final template method defines an algorithm skeleton while subclasses supply specific steps. You’ll learn when that pattern is preferable to Strategy. Fourth, explain how Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control enable OCP by moving control of object creation out of the client. You will recognize DI as a testability and extensibility enabler and know simple ways to inject dependencies. Each objective pairs a skill with why it matters and a small visual cue to help memory. Think about a class in your codebase that receives many conditionals — that’s your first candidate for these techniques.

keyIdea.title: Skills to practice

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Learning Objectives
Refactoring steps (mnemonic: A.D.I.D.)
  • Abstraction: define an interface for the variable behavior.
  • Delegation: have the client call the abstraction instead of branching.
  • Injection: pass a concrete implementation into the client.
  • Decide: choose or configure the strategy at composition time.
Pitfalls & checks
• Only introduce interfaces where change is likely.
• Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies.
• Remember: Template controls structure; Strategy controls variable steps.
Quick practice tip
Pick a class with multiple conditionals. Identify the varying behavior, extract an interface with a single method, implement a concrete class, and inject it. Run tests and verify no edits were needed to the original client.

screens.title: Polymorphism and Abstraction as OCP tools
screens.subtitle: Why depending on interfaces keeps classes closed for modification

narration.text: Polymorphism is the mechanism that allows an object to present different behaviors under a common type. Abstraction is the design technique of defining that common type as an interface or abstract class. Together they create a powerful OCP tool: if a class depends on an abstraction, you can add new concrete types later without changing the dependent class. Concretely, if your OrderProcessor expects a PaymentMethod interface, any new payment implementation becomes an extension, not a change. A common misconception is thinking you should abstract everything. That leads to needless complexity and harder navigation. Instead, pick the seams where behavior varies or is likely to change, like external integrations, business rules, or algorithms. Example: the PaymentProcessor that originally used an if-else to select payment types becomes OCP-compliant by introducing PaymentMethod and letting implementations handle their specifics. This change reduces the surface for regressions because the processor's logic no longer needs edits when a new payment method is added. To practice, look for classes that branch on type or mode — those are candidates for an interface. Takeaway: abstraction plus polymorphism gives you controlled extension points; use them sparingly and intentionally.

keyIdea.title: Why this matters
keyIdea.text: Abstraction + polymorphism let you add behaviors by adding classes, not editing existing clients, reducing risk and simplifying maintenance.

content.html:
Core Concept
Polymorphism & Abstraction
Define interfaces or abstract classes where behavior varies, and have clients depend on them.
Definition
Polymorphism: objects of different classes are treated through a common type. Abstraction: the common type that hides details.
Example (concept)
If PaymentProcessor accepts PaymentMethod, adding BankTransferPayment requires no change to PaymentProcessor.
Common mistake
Abstracting everything. Only extract interfaces where extension is likely or beneficial.
Illustration: move from conditionals to interface
// Abstraction
public interface PaymentMethod {
  void processPayment(double amount);
}

// Concrete implementations
public class CreditCardPayment implements PaymentMethod { ... }
public class PayPalPayment implements PaymentMethod { ... }

// Client depends on abstraction
public class OcpPaymentProcessor {
  private PaymentMethod paymentMethod;
  public OcpPaymentProcessor(PaymentMethod paymentMethod) { this.paymentMethod = paymentMethod; }
  public void executePayment(double amount) { paymentMethod.processPayment(amount); }
}
Key Takeaway

Depend on a small, focused abstraction to allow new behavior to be added without modifying the client.

screens.title: Refactoring PaymentProcessor to respect OCP
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step Java example converting if-else to Strategy

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete refactor that makes a payment processor OCP-compliant. Imagine an initial class with many if-else branches selecting payment behavior. The refactor has three clear steps. First, extract a small interface for the varying behavior — in our source we call it PaymentMethod with a single processPayment method. Second, implement concrete strategies like CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment that encapsulate their logic. Third, change the processor so it depends on the PaymentMethod interface and receives an implementation via its constructor. This turns the processor into a context: it delegates behavior and never inspects types. A common misconception is that this hides important logic; instead, the logic moves to focused classes with clearer responsibilities. Another practice benefit is testability: you can inject a test double implementing PaymentMethod to verify processor orchestration without invoking external services. Example: to add BankTransferPayment you create a new class implementing PaymentMethod — no edits to OcpPaymentProcessor. That discipline keeps stable code small and predictable. How could you apply these three steps to any conditional-heavy class? Refactoring PaymentProcessor to respect OCP means extract interface, implement strategies, inject into the context — add new behaviors by adding classes, not editing the client.. In practical terms, step-by-step java example converting if-else to strategy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor pattern
keyIdea.text: Extract interface, implement strategies, inject into the context — add new behaviors by adding classes, not editing the client.

content.html:
Refactor walkthrough
From branches to strategies
Follow three practical steps: extract abstraction, create concrete strategy classes, and inject the chosen strategy into the processor.
Step 1 — Extract
Define PaymentMethod with processPayment; keep it minimal to avoid over-abstracting.
Step 2 — Implement
Create CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, etc., each containing only its specific logic.
Step 3 — Inject
Have OcpPaymentProcessor receive a PaymentMethod and delegate process calls; add new payments by adding classes.
Code example
// Context receives a strategy
public class OcpPaymentProcessor {
  private PaymentMethod paymentMethod;
  public OcpPaymentProcessor(PaymentMethod paymentMethod) {
    this.paymentMethod = paymentMethod;
  }
  public void executePayment(double amount) {
    paymentMethod.processPayment(amount);
  }
}

// Add a new option without editing the context:
public class BankTransferPayment implements PaymentMethod {
  @Override
  public void processPayment(double amount) {
    System.out.println("Processing Bank Transfer of $" + amount);
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Small, focused interfaces plus concrete classes make adding behavior safe and localize change.

screens.title: Strategy Pattern: encapsulate interchangeable algorithms
screens.subtitle: When and how Strategy supports OCP

narration.text: The Strategy Pattern is ideal when you have a family of algorithms or behaviors that should be interchangeable. It defines a strategy interface and encapsulates each algorithm in a separate class. The client, or context, holds a reference to the strategy and delegates calls to it. This separation makes the context closed for modification: to add a new algorithm you simply add a new concrete strategy. Use Strategy when the variation is primarily in an algorithm or behavior, and when clients may need to switch algorithms at runtime. Strategy differs from Template Method in that Strategy encapsulates whole algorithms as separate objects, while Template Method fixes the overall algorithm and defers steps to subclasses. A common mistake is using Strategy to hide stateful logic that should remain in the context; keep strategies focused and stateless where possible. Example: PaymentMethod is a strategy interface; concrete strategies implement payment processing. Practice choosing between Strategy and Template by asking whether you need multiple independent algorithm objects (Strategy) or a stable flow with varying steps (Template Method). Strategy Pattern: encapsulate interchangeable algorithms means encapsulate algorithms as interchangeable objects and inject them into the context to add new behaviors without editing the client.. In practical terms, when and how strategy supports ocp. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Strategy summary
keyIdea.text: Encapsulate algorithms as interchangeable objects and inject them into the context to add new behaviors without editing the client.

content.html:
Design Pattern
Strategy Pattern
Encapsulate each algorithm in its own class and make them interchangeable via a common interface.
When to use
When you have multiple algorithms that vary independently and may be selected at runtime.
Misconception
Don’t use Strategy to hide context state; strategies should focus on the varying behavior.
Process: how Strategy implements OCP
1
Define the strategy interface with required behavior.
2
Create concrete strategy classes implementing the interface.
3
Inject the chosen strategy into the context; delegate calls.
Example

PaymentMethod is the strategy interface; each payment option is a concrete strategy injected into the processor.

screens.title: Template Method Pattern and OCP
screens.subtitle: When a stable algorithm skeleton is the right choice

narration.text: The Template Method Pattern is useful when the overall sequence of steps is stable but one or more steps vary between implementations. You put the fixed sequence in a final method in the base class, and mark the varying steps as abstract or overridable. Subclasses then implement only those steps. For example, AbstractReportGenerator defines generateAndExportReport as the final template method and defers formatData and exportReport to subclasses. This respects OCP because adding a new report type means adding a subclass, leaving the template untouched. A frequent confusion is choosing between Template Method and Strategy. Use Template when you need to guarantee an ordered flow with hooks, such as setup, process, and teardown. Use Strategy when the variation is a standalone algorithm the context can simply delegate. Another benefit of Template is reuse of shared steps, but beware of deeply coupling subclasses through inherited state — keep the base class minimal and the abstract steps focused. Try thinking in terms of “what must never change?” and keep those parts in the template. Template Method Pattern and OCP means use template method for stable flows with variable steps; add new behaviors by creating subclasses that implement the deferred steps.. In practical terms, when a stable algorithm skeleton is the right choice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Template takeaway
keyIdea.text: Use Template Method for stable flows with variable steps; add new behaviors by creating subclasses that implement the deferred steps.

content.html:
Design Pattern
Template Method
Define an algorithm skeleton and let subclasses implement specific steps without changing the skeleton.
When to use
When you want consistent control flow and allow subclasses to supply step implementations.
Misconception
Avoid putting too much responsibility in the base class; that creates rigid hierarchies.
Code example
public abstract class AbstractReportGenerator {
  public final void generateAndExportReport() {
    String data = fetchData();
    String formatted = formatData(data);
    exportReport(formatted);
  }
  protected String fetchData() { return "Raw Report Data"; }
  protected abstract String formatData(String rawData);
  protected abstract void exportReport(String formattedData);
}

public class PdfReportGenerator extends AbstractReportGenerator { ... }
Key Takeaway

Choose Template Method when control flow must remain stable and extension points are individual steps.

screens.title: Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control
screens.subtitle: How DI/IoC enable OCP and loose coupling

narration.text: Dependency Injection is a practical technique where a class receives the objects it depends on from the outside, typically via constructor parameters. Inversion of Control is the broader idea that the control of creating and wiring objects moves out of application code, often to a container or configuration point. Together they enable OCP by letting clients depend on abstractions while composition decides which concrete implementations to provide. For example, an OrderProcessor that requires an IEmailSender can receive either SmtpEmailService or AwsSesEmailService without code changes. This separation improves testability: in tests you inject a fake or mock implementation. A common misconception is that DI requires a heavy framework; simple constructor injection achieves the benefits without complexity. When designing for OCP, prefer constructor injection for required dependencies and keep composition at application startup. Also avoid using DI to hide unclear object lifecycles; be explicit about ownership and scope. In short, DI/IoC move binding decisions to composition, so domain classes remain closed to modification while open to extension through provided implementations. Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control means inject dependencies to swap implementations without editing clients; composition controls which concrete classes are used.. In practical terms, how di/ioc enable ocp and loose coupling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DI helps OCP
keyIdea.text: Inject dependencies to swap implementations without editing clients; composition controls which concrete classes are used.

content.html:
Enabler
Dependency Injection & IoC
Move instantiation and wiring out of the class so clients remain dependent only on abstractions.
Benefits
Loose coupling, easier testing, and the ability to swap implementations at composition time.
Practical tip
Use constructor injection for required dependencies and keep the composition root simple and explicit.
Architecture: composition vs. client code
Composition root
Place wiring logic where the app boots, not in domain classes. This keeps domain code stable and testable.
// Constructor injection example
public class OrderProcessor {
  private final IEmailSender emailSender;
  public OrderProcessor(IEmailSender emailSender) { this.emailSender = emailSender; }
  // uses emailSender without creating it
}

// Composition
IEmailSender sender = new SmtpEmailService();
OrderProcessor processor = new OrderProcessor(sender);
Common mistake

Avoid creating many transient objects inside domain classes; it couples creation to usage and blocks extension.

screens.title: Strategy vs Template Method
screens.subtitle: How to choose between the two patterns for OCP

narration.text: Choosing between Strategy and Template Method often confuses engineers. Think of Strategy as a collection of interchangeable algorithms encapsulated in separate objects that a client can swap at runtime. Template Method, on the other hand, fixes the control flow in a base class while letting subclasses override specific steps. A practical way to choose: ask whether the variation is a self-contained algorithm you want to swap wholesale. If yes, use Strategy. If the variation is a single step or hook in a larger, stable flow, Template Method is a better fit. For example, swapping different payment processors is a natural Strategy use case; varying only how data is formatted inside a stable reporting flow fits Template Method. Common misconceptions include using Template Method to avoid interfaces — Template still creates coupling through inheritance. Also, Strategy may be overkill if you only need two trivial variants; keep simplicity in mind. The key is to match the pattern to the kind of variation: whole-algorithm variation calls for Strategy, fixed-flow-with-steps calls for Template Method. Strategy vs Template Method means use strategy for interchangeable algorithms; use template method for stable flows with overridable steps.. In practical terms, how to choose between the two patterns for ocp. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Use Strategy for interchangeable algorithms; use Template Method for stable flows with overridable steps.

content.html:
Comparison
Strategy
Interchangeable algorithms encapsulated as objects.
  • Best when algorithms vary independently.
  • Clients choose or are injected with a strategy.
  • Good for runtime swapping and testing.
Comparison
Template Method
Stable control flow with variable steps implemented by subclasses.
  • Best when the sequence of steps must be preserved.
  • Subclasses override specific steps.
  • Good for reuse of shared steps across variants.
Quick decision checklist
Is the variation a whole algorithm? → Strategy
Is the flow fixed but steps vary? → Template
Will runtime swapping or injection be needed? → Strategy

screens.title: Hands-on: Implementing Strategy for Shipping Cost
screens.subtitle: Guided steps to build the shipping strategy calculator

narration.text: This hands-on activity asks you to implement the Strategy Pattern for shipping cost calculation. The goal is to create an IShippingStrategy interface with a calculate(Order) method and three concrete strategies: Standard, Express, and International. The ShippingCostCalculator should accept an IShippingStrategy through its constructor and delegate the calculation. Start by defining the interface as a single-method contract; keep it minimal. Implement StandardShippingStrategy using the formula five dollars plus one dollar fifty per kilogram, Express as ten dollars plus three dollars per kilogram, and International as twenty dollars plus five dollars per kilogram for non-USA destinations. Next, create the ShippingCostCalculator class that holds an IShippingStrategy and exposes a calculate(Order) method delegating to the strategy. Test in main by instantiating different strategies and injecting them into the calculator. A common pitfall is putting rate logic back into the calculator; keep rates inside the strategies. After implementation, consider how DI would let you swap strategies in production or tests. This exercise reinforces extracting an interface, injecting strategies, and keeping the context unchanged as you add new shipping methods. Hands-on: Implementing Strategy for Shipping Cost means build ishippingstrategy implementations and inject them into shippingcostcalculator to practice ocp via strategy and di.. In practical terms, guided steps to build the shipping strategy calculator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Exercise goal
keyIdea.text: Build IShippingStrategy implementations and inject them into ShippingCostCalculator to practice OCP via Strategy and DI.

content.html:
Practical Exercise
Shipping Strategy Steps
  1. Define interface IShippingStrategy with calculate(Order).
  2. Implement Standard, Express, and International strategies.
  3. Create ShippingCostCalculator that receives an IShippingStrategy in its constructor.
  4. Test by injecting different strategies and calling calculate.
Keep rate logic inside strategies and the calculator as a thin delegator to remain OCP-compliant.
Starter hints
// Interface
public interface IShippingStrategy {
  double calculate(Order order);
}

// Example strategy
public class StandardShippingStrategy implements IShippingStrategy {
  public double calculate(Order order) { return 5.0 + 1.5 * order.getWeight(); }
}

// Calculator (context)
public class ShippingCostCalculator {
  private IShippingStrategy strategy;
  public ShippingCostCalculator(IShippingStrategy strategy) { this.strategy = strategy; }
  public double calculate(Order order) { return strategy.calculate(order); }
}
Pro tip

Write unit tests for each strategy; this keeps algorithm rules clear and independent.

screens.title: Starter Code Walkthrough for Shipping Activity
screens.subtitle: Examine the Order class and how to wire strategies in main

narration.text: Read the starter code carefully before you implement strategies. The Order class provides weight and destination; your IShippingStrategy will consume that information. In main you will create orders, instantiate a strategy, inject it into ShippingCostCalculator, and print results. Keep the calculator implementation minimal — it should only call the injected strategy. When testing, you can inject a dummy strategy that returns a predictable value to confirm wiring. A common mistake is reading destination logic incorrectly; InternationalShippingStrategy must check the order's destination and apply its formula only when the destination is not USA. Also, avoid duplicating rate formulas across strategies — each strategy owns its own formula. After implementing, run the example usage to verify outputs for domestic and international orders. This walkthrough explains intent rather than giving the full solution so you can apply OCP thinking during implementation and keep the client code unchanged when adding new shipping types. Starter Code Walkthrough for Shipping Activity means the order class is immutable for this activity; strategies read its values and return a calculated cost without side effects.. In practical terms, examine the order class and how to wire strategies in main. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Walkthrough note
keyIdea.text: The Order class is immutable for this activity; strategies read its values and return a calculated cost without side effects.

content.html:
Code Example
Order class (given)
class Order {
  private double weight;
  private String destinationCountry;
  public Order(double weight, String destinationCountry) {
    this.weight = weight;
    this.destinationCountry = destinationCountry;
  }
  public double getWeight() { return weight; }
  public String getDestinationCountry() { return destinationCountry; }
}
The Order class gives the data strategies need. Keep your strategy code focused on calculation and free of external I/O.
Main usage sketch
public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    Order domestic = new Order(2.5, "USA");
    Order international = new Order(5.0, "Germany");

    ShippingCostCalculator calc = new ShippingCostCalculator(new StandardShippingStrategy());
    System.out.println("Standard: $" + calc.calculate(domestic));

    calc = new ShippingCostCalculator(new InternationalShippingStrategy());
    System.out.println("International: $" + calc.calculate(international));
  }
}
Check your understanding

Does your International strategy verify the destination before applying its formula? That prevents incorrect charges for domestic orders.

screens.title: Practical rules and anti-patterns for OCP
screens.subtitle: How to apply patterns without over-engineering

narration.text: Applying OCP well is as much about restraint as it is about design. Apply these practical rules: prefer small, focused interfaces with a single responsibility; keep abstractions minimal to avoid coupling many classes together; use constructor injection for required dependencies and setters for optional ones. Watch for anti-patterns: creating interfaces for every class, which adds noise and cognitive overhead; hiding significant logic behind many indirections; and using inheritance to share unrelated behavior. When refactoring towards OCP, work incrementally: extract an interface, move the varying code into a concrete class, run tests, and only then replace other callers. Use tests to ensure behavior remains unchanged during the refactor. When in doubt between Strategy and Template Method, consult the decision checklist: does the variation represent a whole algorithm or a single step? Finally, remember OCP is about managing change: you will sometimes modify code for bug fixes — OCP aims to minimize edits for new features, not eliminate edits entirely. Practical rules and anti-patterns for OCP means be pragmatic: favor minimal interfaces, incremental refactors, and tests to keep ocp benefits without over-engineering.. In practical terms, how to apply patterns without over-engineering. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical rules
keyIdea.text: Be pragmatic: favor minimal interfaces, incremental refactors, and tests to keep OCP benefits without over-engineering.

content.html:
Best Practices
Rules of thumb for practical OCP
Minimal interfaces
Design small contracts with one responsibility to limit coupling.
Incremental refactor
Extract, move logic, test, then replace callers to keep risk low.
Test-driven verification
Use unit tests and test doubles to validate behavior after refactor.
Anti-pattern: over-abstraction
Avoid creating unused interfaces for classes that will never vary.
Own composition
Keep wiring at the composition root to preserve clarity and control.
Clarify ownership
Document which component owns a dependency and its lifecycle to avoid surprises.

narration.text: These are the concise concepts to take away. Polymorphism lets objects of different types be treated through a common interface, enabling extension without edits. Abstraction provides the contract — a small interface or abstract class — that clients rely on. The Strategy Pattern packages algorithms into interchangeable objects so you can add new behavior by adding classes. The Template Method Pattern fixes the overall flow and delegates specific steps to subclasses, useful when order matters. Dependency Injection and IoC move object creation into composition, allowing clients to remain closed to changes in concrete implementations. Finally, watch for over-abstraction: only introduce interfaces where change is likely. Use tests and small, incremental refactors to realize OCP benefits in real systems. Key Concepts means design for extension with focused abstractions, choose the right pattern, and use di to wire implementations safely.. In practical terms, what to remember. narration.text: A few final terms to lock in. Template Method defines a final algorithm structure and defers steps to subclasses so you can add new types by subclassing. Dependency Injection is the practice of providing dependencies from the outside so classes remain unaware of concrete implementations. Inversion of Control is the principle that shifts responsibility for object creation away from application logic into a dedicated composition layer. Practically, these tools let you add new behavior by creating new classes and wiring them, rather than editing existing code — which is the essence of OCP. The final question to ask when you refactor is: can I add a new behavior by adding code, not changing the client? If yes, you’ve achieved OCP for that concern.
